title: Olá e Adeus / Greetings and farewells
bridge: In Spanish, 'hola' and 'adiós' are used in almost all contexts, but in Portuguese there are important nuances. For example, 'Olá' is a general greeting, but 'Bom dia' (good morning) is used until midday, and 'Boa tarde' (good afternoon) from midday until evening. Be careful: 'Boa noite' is used both to greet and to say goodbye at night, but 'boa madrugada' is not used as a greeting. Additionally, in Portuguese, 'tchau' (of Italian origin) is very common for saying goodbye, while 'adeus' sounds formal and definitive. Pay attention to pronunciation: the final 'o' in 'Olá' is pronounced like a closed 'a', and the 'e' in 'tchau' does not exist; it is pronounced 'tchau' with 'au' as in 'auto'.
rule:
In Portuguese, greetings and farewells are chosen based on the time of day and level of formality. At the A1 level, it is essential to master the following forms:

- General greetings: 'Olá' (hello), 'Oi' (hi, more informal).
- Time-based greetings: 'Bom dia' (good morning, until 12:00), 'Boa tarde' (good afternoon, from 12:00 until evening), 'Boa noite' (good evening/night, to greet or say goodbye when it is already night).
- Farewells: 'Tchau' (bye, informal and common), 'Adeus' (goodbye, formal, used when you do not expect to see the person again), 'Até logo' (see you later), 'Até amanhã' (see you tomorrow), 'Até já' (see you in a moment, very soon).
- In formal contexts, you can also use 'Como está?' (how are you?) or 'Como vai?' (how’s it going?), but at the A1 level, it is enough to use 'Tudo bem?' (all good?) as a greeting and response.
- The typical response to 'Tudo bem?' is 'Tudo bem' or 'Tudo ótimo' (all great).
- Remember that in Portuguese, 'buenos días' is not used to say goodbye; for farewells, use forms with 'até'.
- Intonation is important: 'Oi' sounds friendlier than 'Olá', and 'Tchau' is pronounced with the diphthong 'au', not like 'chao'.

common_error.explanation: The most common mistake is to transfer 'buenos días' literally into Portuguese, but in Portuguese the expression is 'bom dia' in the singular and without the 's'. Additionally, 'dias' is pronounced 'dʒiɐs' and 'dia' is pronounced 'dʒiɐ'. To avoid this, practice the pronunciation and memorize the singular form. It is also common to use 'hola' as 'hola' in Portuguese, but the correct form is 'olá' or 'oi'.

examples.note: General and neutral greeting. Can be used in any context.
More informal than 'olá', used among friends and acquaintances.
Used until 12 noon. The 'o' in 'bom' is nasalized.
Very common in Brazil, pronounced with the diphthong 'au'.
Used when you expect to see the person soon.
Used when you will see the person the next day.
Used from midday until evening (approximately until 6-7 PM).
Used both to greet and to say goodbye when it is already night.
Very common informal greeting, used like 'how’s it going?'.

title: Apresentar-se e apresentar outros / Introducing yourself and others
bridge: In Spanish, you say 'me llamo' and 'te presento a...', while in Portuguese the form 'chamar-se' (to be called) is used with reflexive pronouns: 'eu me chamo' (I am called) and 'ele se chama' (he is called). When introducing others, the most common expression is 'te apresento' (I introduce you) or 'esta é a...' (this is...). Be careful: do not use 'me llamo' directly; in Portuguese it is 'me chamo' or 'o meu nome é' (my name is).
rule: In Portuguese, to say your name you use the reflexive verb 'chamar-se' (to be called) or the expression 'o meu nome é' (my name is). With 'chamar-se', it conjugates as follows: eu me chamo, você se chama, ele/ela se chama, nós nos chamamos, vocês se chamam, eles/elas se chamam. To introduce someone, use 'te apresento' or 'esta/este é' (this is). For example: 'Te apresento o João' (I introduce you to João). You can also say 'esta é a Maria' (this is María). Remember that in Portuguese, unlike Spanish, the definite article is used before proper names in informal contexts (a Maria, o João), although it is optional.

concept_examples.text: Este é o meu amigo Pedro.

common_error.explanation: The error occurs because Spanish speakers tend to use the structure 'me llamo' directly, but in Portuguese the reflexive verb 'chamar-se' requires the pronoun 'me' after the subject. Additionally, it is common to omit the subject 'eu', but it is necessary to conjugate the verb correctly. Remember that in Portuguese you say 'eu me chamo' or 'o meu nome é'.

levels.label: Dizer o próprio nome / Decir el propio nombre

examples.note: Use of the reflexive verb 'chamar-se' with pronoun 'me'.
Formal alternative: 'o meu nome é' + name.

levels.label: Perguntar o nome de alguém / Preguntar el nombre de alguien

examples.note: Use of 'como' (how) + reflexive verb. Do not use 'cómo te llamas' literally.
Another common and polite form.

levels.label: Apresentar outras pessoas / Presentar a otras personas

examples.translation: I introduce you to my sister.
examples.note: Use of 'te apresento' + a + person. Be careful: do not say 'te presento a mi hermana' with 'a' in front.

examples.original: Esta é a minha amiga Carla.
examples.note: Use of 'esta é' to introduce a woman. The optional definite article is used.

title: Dizer de onde você é / Say where you're from
bridge: In Portuguese, to ask where someone is from, you use 'De onde você é?' In Spanish, it would be '¿De dónde eres?', but note that Portuguese uses the preposition 'de' contracted with 'onde' (de + onde = de onde), while in Spanish we use 'de dónde'. Also, the verb 'ser' is conjugated similarly: 'você é' (you are, formal/informal in Brazil), but be careful with 'tu és' (you are) used in Portugal and some regions of Brazil. The word 'nacionalidade' (nationality) is spelled almost the same, but the pronunciation differs. The main challenge for Spanish speakers is not to confuse the use of 'ser' vs. 'estar' – in Portuguese, origin is always expressed with 'ser', just like in Spanish, but remember that 'você' takes the third-person singular conjugation: 'você é' (you are), not 'você eres'.
rule: To ask and say where you're from in Portuguese, we use the verb 'ser' (to be) in the present indicative. The forms are: eu sou (I am), tu és (you are – used in Portugal/formal Brazil), você é (you are – in Brazil), ele/ela é (he/she is), nós somos (we are), vocês são (you all are), eles/elas são (they are). The typical question is 'De onde você é?' (Where are you from? – in Brazil). To answer, we use 'Eu sou de + place' (I'm from + place) or 'Eu sou + nationality' (I'm + nationality). Examples: 'Eu sou do Brasil' (I'm from Brazil – note the contraction de+o = do), 'Eu sou de Portugal' (I'm from Portugal – no contraction because 'Portugal' doesn't take an article). Nationality is expressed with the corresponding adjective: 'brasileiro/a', 'português/portuguesa', 'espanhol/a', etc. Note that in Portuguese, nationality adjectives are written with lowercase letters. To ask directly about nationality, you can say 'Qual é a sua nacionalidade?' (What is your nationality?) or 'Você é de onde?' – the latter is more colloquial and the word order differs from Spanish. Remember that with 'você', you always use the third-person singular conjugation: 'você é', not 'você és'. In Brazil, the 'tu' form is often conjugated as 'tu é' in colloquial speech, but in formal contexts 'você é' is preferred. For A1, focus on the forms with 'você' and 'eu'.

concept_examples.translation: ¿De dónde eres? (in Brazil, used for tú/usted)

common_error.correct_alt: Tu és de onde? (in Portugal or formal Brazil)
common_error.explanation: The error occurs because in Spanish we use 'tú eres' and the student transfers the 'és' form to 'você'. But in Portuguese, 'você' requires the third-person singular conjugation: 'é'. The 'tu' form is only used with the 'és' conjugation in European Portuguese or formal contexts in Brazil. In Brazil, people often say 'tu é' in colloquial speech, but the standard form prefers 'você é'. To avoid the error, remember that 'você' is like 'usted' in Spanish, so always use the third-person singular form.

examples.note: This is the standard question in Brazil. Notice that 'de onde' means 'where from' and is used at the beginning.
In Portuguese, when we ask with 'de onde' at the end, it sounds more colloquial and emphatic. The structure is: subject + verb + de onde.
Here we use 'de que' instead of 'de onde' to ask specifically about the country. 'de que' = 'of what'.
The contraction 'do' = 'de' + 'o' (article). In Spanish we say 'de México' without an article, but in Portuguese we use 'do' because 'México' takes the definite article 'o' in Portuguese: 'o México'.
Here we use 'da' = 'de' + 'a' (feminine article). 'Espanha' takes the article 'a' in Portuguese: 'a Espanha'.
With countries that don't take an article (like Angola, Portugal, Brazil – though Brazil is often used with 'o Brasil'), we use just 'de' without contraction.
Nationality adjectives in Portuguese are written in lowercase. 'Brasileiro' ends in -o for masculine.
Notice the ending -a for feminine. Some countries have specific forms, like 'argentino/a', 'chileno/a', etc.
Remember that plural adjectives end in -s, and the masculine plural is -os. You can also use 'a gente é' instead of 'nós somos' in colloquial speech.

translations.en: Asking and saying where you're from / Origin and nationality
